title: The Questions You Won't Ask
author: The Best Leadership Newsletter
summary: The author uses the figure of the conspiracy theorist to diagnose a specific blind spot in leaders: the willingness to question everything outside their own identity while refusing to question beliefs that reinforce their self-image. Conspiracy theorists are not characterized by excessive questioning but by the point at which they stop — when the evidence would threaten what they are certain about. Leaders do the same thing: they scrutinize market conditions, team execution, and timelines but cannot question the strategy, the style, or the identity that produced those decisions, because doing so would mean questioning themselves. A VP case study illustrates the pattern with precision: after a failed product launch, the leader blamed every external variable except the strategy itself, because the strategy was his, and questioning it meant questioning his judgment as a savvy leader. The author proposes two diagnostic questions that the conspiracy theorist will not ask and that most leaders also avoid: 'What if I'm wrong?' and 'What am I protecting by not questioning myself?' The questions most needed are precisely the ones the unexamined leader refuses to ask.
points: The conspiracy theorist and the unexamined leader share the same cognitive failure — certainty that prevents questioning — disguised as principled skepticism that stops at a conveniently self-serving boundary.

Questions stop at the edge of identity: leaders will question anything that threatens their point of view but protect anything that reinforces their self-image, making their beliefs structurally indistinguishable from the conspiracy theories they would dismiss in others.

The VP case study makes the pattern concrete: after a failed product launch, the leader blamed market, team, and timeline in a group debrief without questioning the strategy he had spent three months developing, because doing so would mean questioning his identity as a savvy leader.

Confirmation bias runs both ways — leaders remember wins that validate their judgment and forget losses that question it, consciously or not always looking for evidence that confirms what they already believe and dismissing evidence that contradicts it.

The diagnostic move is simple but most leaders will not take it: ask 'What am I protecting by not questioning myself?' — the question both the conspiracy theorist and the unreflective leader alike refuse to entertain.
quotes: You’ll question anything, as long as it threatens your point of view. But you’ll protect anything that reinforces your self-image.
The challenge is not that they question things. The challenge is that they are so certain of their beliefs, they stop questioning.

In the group debrief, the VP blamed the market because market conditions had changed. He blamed the team because they didn’t execute the way he thought they should. He blamed the timeline because the strategy would’ve worked if they had just a little more runway. The only thing the VP didn’t blame in that meeting was the strategy itself.

Your brain does the exact same thing. You’ll remember the wins that validate your business prowess and forget the losses that question it. Consciously or not, you are always looking for evidence to confirm what you already believe and you’ll dismiss the evidence that contradicts it.
Your beliefs are conspiracy theories you’ve convinced yourself are facts. The only difference is that you can’t see the conspiracy you created.
The conspiracy theorist won’t ask those questions. But you’re not a conspiracy theorist, right? Just remember, the questions you won’t ask are usually the ones you most need to answer.
